findings.statement: Broadcom's AI XPU platform comprises custom ASIC accelerators (AI XPUs) designed for AI inference workloads in data‑center and cloud environments. The company markets these AI XPUs as part of its AI infrastructure portfolio and has secured multi‑year orders for AI racks built around the XPU accelerators.

Broadcom delivers its AI capabilities through a subscription‑based licensing model via VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF). VCF 9.0, released for FY 26, includes VMware Private AI Services as a standard component of the VCF subscription, removing the need for separate perpetual AI product licenses.

Broadcom’s AI infrastructure portfolio includes custom AI accelerators that are optimized for low power consumption and high performance, as well as merchant silicon connectivity solutions such as Ethernet and PCIe components. These hardware offerings are positioned for deployment in data‑center and cloud AI workloads, enabling large‑scale AI clusters.

Broadcom has an expanded partnership with Google Cloud that optimizes Broadcom’s VMware‑based AI solutions for Google Cloud and adds them to the Google Cloud Marketplace. The announcement is presented as a global initiative, indicating deployment of Broadcom AI computing solutions on Google Cloud in both the United States and Europe where Google Cloud operates.

Broadcom’s licensing model for AI‑related software (e.g., VMware Cloud Foundation and VMware Private AI Foundation) uses a subscription‑based approach with primary licenses for core platforms and add‑on licenses that provide additional capacity such as vSAN or AI foundation add‑ons. License capacity aggregates across active subscriptions, and usage analytics are available for customers to monitor consumption.

AMD Instinct GPUs are offered through several cloud service providers: Microsoft Azure (ND MI300X v5 instances) and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (BM.GPU.MI300X.8 bare‑metal) provide AMD Instinct at scale in both United States and European regions; IBM Cloud, Aligned, Cirrascale, TensorWave and Vultr also deliver AMD Instinct‑based instances globally. In Europe, Nscale operates a GPU cluster powered by Instinct MI250X accelerators in its Glomfjord data centre in Norway.

AMD’s AI‑focused hardware portfolio for cloud and data‑center workloads includes the Instinct MI455X and MI430X GPUs (part of the MI400 series), the Instinct MI350P PCIe accelerator cards, 6th‑generation EPYC™ server CPUs, the Helios AI rack‑scale solution, Ryzen™ AI Embedded X100 processors for edge/embedded AI, and the Kria™ AI System‑on‑Module and robotics developer platform.

AMD: Microsoft, a United States‑based cloud service provider, has deployed AMD Helios AI rack‑scale systems for its AI workloads. In Europe, the French sovereign‑cloud provider Scaleway has integrated AMD’s 5th‑generation EPYC server CPUs into its bare‑metal and AI service offerings.

Intel Corp: Intel’s AI compute portfolio for data‑center and cloud AI workloads includes its Xeon Scalable processors (including Xeon CPU Max), the Gaudi family of AI accelerators (Gaudi 2 and the newly announced Gaudi 3 PCIe card and 32‑node cluster), Intel Arc Pro GPUs and Data Center GPU Flex series. These products are positioned for both training and inference workloads and are integrated with Intel’s oneAPI and OpenVINO software stack to enable optimized performance. The Gaudi accelerators are offered in a standard PCIe Gen5 form factor and support Ethernet‑based scaling.

Intel Corp: Amazon Web Services (AWS) offers Intel‑based Habana Gaudi AI accelerators through its EC2 DL1 instance type, which is currently available in the United States East (Northern Virginia) and West (Oregon) regions and supports on‑demand, reserved, spot and savings‑plan pricing. IBM Cloud also provides access to Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerators, extending Intel’s AI hardware presence in the cloud (regional coverage not specified). Intel’s partner listings confirm the AWS‑Gaudi integration for the Americas region.

Intel Corp: Intel’s AI hardware is monetized through cloud‑based usage models: AWS EC2 DL1 instances powered by Gaudi accelerators are sold on an on‑demand, reserved, spot or savings‑plan basis, providing flexible consumption pricing. Additionally, Intel’s AI software tools are offered under free‑license terms for a limited period, as described in its licensing FAQ.

Intel Corp: Intel currently offers a portfolio of AI compute products for cloud and data‑center workloads, including the 4th Gen Intel Xeon Scalable processors (available on AWS, GCP, Azure), the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series (up to 128 Xe cores, >500 TOPS), the Intel Data Center GPU Flex Series (Flex 140, Flex 170, Flex 170V with 16‑32 Xe cores and an industry‑first AV1 encoder), and a unified software stack via oneAPI toolkits (AI Analytics Toolkit, oneDNN, oneMKL, etc.) that enable optimized AI inference and training across CPUs and GPUs.

Intel Corp: Intel’s 4th Gen Xeon Scalable processors are offered as preview instances on Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud Platform and Microsoft Azure, and are generally available on Alibaba Cloud; benchmark data show deployments on Azure US‑West and US‑East regions, confirming active use in United States data centers. Intel also partners with AWS, Cisco, Ericsson and Nokia to deliver private 5G solutions that incorporate Intel AI hardware, extending availability to Europe and the United States.

Intel Corp: Intel’s Data Center GPU Flex Series is sold under a recommended‑customer pricing model; Intel cites “up to 50 % lower total‑cost‑of‑ownership for VDI” as of 11 Oct 2023 compared with competing solutions. The oneAPI software toolkits are distributed under the Intel End User License Agreement (EULA) with component‑specific third‑party licenses, providing a royalty‑free, usage‑based licensing model for developers.

Broadcom sells its custom AI XPU ASICs as fully packaged chips directly to hyperscale cloud providers, indicating that the company not only designs but also delivers completed AI accelerator units to customers such as Google and AWS.
Broadcom reported AI semiconductor revenue of $10.8 billion in Q2 FY2026, a 143 % year‑over‑year increase, demonstrating a sizable revenue presence in the AI compute segment across its key markets.

AMD: The Instinct MI400 series, launched in 2026, includes the MI455X GPU for training and inference and the MI430X GPU for HPC. Both deliver up to 40 PFLOP (FP4) and 20 PFLOP (FP8) compute, feature HBM4 memory, and use the CDNA 5 architecture, representing a roughly two‑fold performance increase over the prior MI350 series.

AMD announced the Instinct MI500 series of AI accelerators, slated for launch in 2027. Built on the next‑generation CDNA 6 architecture, the MI500 GPUs will use a 2 nm process, HBM4E memory, and are projected to deliver up to a 1,000× performance uplift versus the MI300X GPUs introduced in 2023.

AMD unveiled the Helios rack‑scale AI platform, a turnkey solution that combines 72 Instinct MI455X GPUs with 18 sixth‑generation EPYC CPUs, integrated Pensando networking, and ROCm software, targeting yotta‑scale AI workloads in data centers.

AMD completed its acquisition of ZT Systems in March 2025 and announced the divestiture of ZT’s server‑manufacturing business for $3 billion, retaining ZT’s rack‑scale AI solutions design assets to accelerate AMD’s own AI infrastructure offerings.

AMD: At the Advancing AI 2026 event AMD introduced the 6th‑generation EPYC 9006 series server CPUs, marketed as the broadest portfolio for agentic AI workloads across cloud, enterprise, and HPC environments.
AMD: IDC’s AI Accelerator Vendor Share report for CY2Q25 shows AMD holding 1.8% of AI accelerator vendor revenue, placing it behind NVIDIA (85.2%) and Broadcom (10.3%).
AMD’s MI300 series GPUs, purpose‑built for AI training and inference, have attracted adoption by major cloud providers seeking alternatives to NVIDIA’s offerings.

Intel Corp: According to a Grand View Research report, Intel captured roughly 32% of the revenue share in the North American AI computer market in 2025, making it one of the leading vendors in the United States AI compute segment. The report does not provide a specific Europe share.

We believe that making the models more widely available will facilitate efforts across the AI community to benefit the world at large. LLMs offer one of the most promising AI technologies to benefit society, given the remarkable capability they have demonstrated in generating text, summarizing and translating content, responding to questions, engaging in conversations, and performing more complicated tasks, such as solving math problems or reasoning. LLMs have the potential to unlock new forms of creativity and insights and inspire passion in the AI community to advance the technology.

Llama 2 is designed to help developers, researchers, and organizations build generative AI-powered tools and experiences. Meta released pretrained and fine-tuned versions of Llama 2 with 7B, 13B, and 70B parameters. With Llama 2, Meta implemented three core safety techniques across the company’s fine-tuned models: supervised safety fine-tuning, targeted safety context distillation, and safety reinforcement learning from human feedback. This has enabled Meta to improve safety performance. By democratizing access, it will allow for continual identification and mitigation of vulnerabilities in a transparent and open manner.

Intel offers a portfolio of AI solutions that provide competitive and compelling options for the community to develop and run models like Llama 2. Gaudi2 is supported by the Habana SynapseAI\* software suite, which integrates PyTorch\* and DeepSpeed\* for both training and inference. Further software optimizations are coming to Gaudi2, including support for the FP8 data type in Q3 2023, which is expected to deliver substantial performance boosts, increasing throughput and reducing latency in LLM execution.

# Accelerate Llama 2 with Intel® AI Hardware and Software Optimizations

Democratizing Access to Large Language Models

![author-image]()

By

**Fan Zhao**, *AI Software Engineering Manager*, **Antony Vance Jeyaraj**, *Cloud Software Architect*, **Sree Ganesan**, *AI Software Engineering Manager*, **Susan Lansing**, *AI Marketing Manager,* **Kristina Kermanshahche**, *Software Product Manager,* **Radhika Rao**, *AI Marketing Manager*, **Patricia Mwove**, *Cloud Software Architect*, and **Andres Rodriguez**, *Intel Fellow*

Intel Corporation

We are excited to see Meta release Llama 2, with the intent to further democratize access to large language models (LLMs). We believe that making the models more widely available will facilitate efforts across the AI community to benefit the world at large. LLMs offer one of the most promising AI technologies to benefit society, given the remarkable capability they have demonstrated in generating text, summarizing and translating content, responding to questions, engaging in conversations, and performing more complicated tasks, such as solving math problems or reasoning. LLMs have the potential to unlock new forms of creativity and insights and inspire passion in the AI community to advance the technology.

Llama 2 is designed to help developers, researchers, and organizations build generative AI-powered tools and experiences. Meta released pretrained and fine-tuned versions of Llama 2 with 7B, 13B, and 70B parameters. With Llama 2, Meta implemented three core safety techniques across the company’s fine-tuned models: supervised safety fine-tuning, targeted safety context distillation, and safety reinforcement learning from human feedback. This has enabled Meta to improve safety performance. By democratizing access, it will allow for continual identification and mitigation of vulnerabilities in a transparent and open manner.

Intel offers a portfolio of AI solutions that provide competitive and compelling options for the community to develop and run models like Llama 2. Intel’s rich hardware portfolio, combined with optimized [open software](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/topic-technology/artificial-intelligence/overview.html), provides alternatives to mitigate the challenge of accessing limited compute resources. With the release of Llama 2, we are happy to share initial inference performance of 7B and 13B parameter models on Intel’s AI portfolio, including Habana Gaudi2\* deep learning accelerator, 4th Gen Intel® Xeon® Scalable processors, Intel® Xeon® CPU Max Series, and Intel® Data Center GPU Max. The results that we share here are for out-of-box performance with our currently released software, with additional performance gains expected in upcoming releases. We are also enabling the 70B parameter model and will provide an update shortly to keep the community informed.

## Habana Gaudi2\* Deep Learning Accelerator

Habana Gaudi2 is designed to provide high-performance, high-efficiency training and inference, and is particularly suited to large language models such as Llama and Llama 2. Each Gaudi2 accelerator features 96 GB of on-chip HBM2E to meet the memory demands of LLMs, thus accelerating inference performance. Gaudi2 is supported by the Habana SynapseAI\* software suite, which integrates PyTorch\* and DeepSpeed\* for both training and inference. Moreover, support for [HPU Graphs](https://docs.habana.ai/en/latest/PyTorch/Inference_on_PyTorch/Inference_Using_HPU_Graphs.html) and [DeepSpeed inference](https://docs.habana.ai/en/latest/PyTorch/DeepSpeed/Inference_Using_DeepSpeed.html) have recently been introduced in SynapseAI, and these are well-suited to latency-sensitive inference applications. Further software optimizations are coming to Gaudi2, including support for the FP8 data type in Q3 2023, which is expected to deliver substantial performance boosts, increasing throughput and reducing latency in LLM execution.

Performance on LLMs requires flexible and nimble scalability to reduce network bottlenecks, both within the server and across nodes. Every Gaudi2 integrates 24 100 GB Ethernet ports; 21 ports can be dedicated to all-to-all connectivity to the eight Gaudi2s within the server and three ports per Gaudi2 dedicated to scale out. This network configuration helps accelerate scaled performance both within and beyond the server.

Gaudi2 has demonstrated excellent training performance on large language models on the recently published [MLPerf\* benchmark](https://mlcommons.org/en/training-normal-30/) for training the 175B parameter GPT-3 model on 384 Gaudi2 accelerators. **What’s New:** Private 5G networks are in high demand in 2024 as enterprises look for scalable compute solutions to power the next wave of artificial intelligence (AI) applications running at the edge and drive their digital transformation efforts. Gartner® predicts that “by 2025 more than 50% of enterprise-managed data will be created and processed outside the data center or cloud.”1 To meet this exceptional demand, Intel has collaborated with several scale companies to give customers access to private 5G solutions and vertical market deployments around the world.

> “By harnessing the breadth of the Intel product portfolio with the integration capabilities and scale of our deep ecosystem, enterprises around the world can reap the benefits of a personalized private network for their business requirements. We are seeing the rapid growth of AI and edge computing combined with the connectivity of 5G drive intelligence, cost savings and innovation across developing and mature industries.”

**Why It Matters:**These deployments culminate years of investment, development, collaboration and lab trials that are now becoming mainstream and setting an example of industry excellence.

Intel, via an end-to-end hardware and software products portfolio (processors, Ethernet, FlexRAN, OpenVINO and 5G core software offerings) and industry collaborations are breaking down the barriers to allow operators to monetize their networks and enterprises to quickly design and deploy intelligent private networks across industry verticals, including manufacturing, transportation hubs, mining, utilities, healthcare, education and others.

As generative AI has presented new potential for enterprise workloads, businesses are working to leverage the intersection of 5G, AI and edge computing in private networks to increase connectivity, data security and efficiencies relative to their specific industry goals and initiatives. Private 5G networks give customers a quick, easy path to delivering high-bandwidth, low-latency compute in secure environments needed for the most demanding edge workloads.

## SUMMARY

How's the AI chip market doing these days? The AI chip market is still doing very well, but the easy, broad phase is over.

The strongest signal is not just Nvidia’s scale. It is that recent evidence points in the same direction across public chip vendors, hyperscaler capex, memory suppliers, AI cloud infrastructure, and semiconductor startup funding.

Money is still rushing into AI chips, but it has become much more selective. Investors are now favoring bottlenecks such as inference, memory bandwidth, non-Nvidia capacity, custom silicon, and deployed AI infrastructure rather than generic accelerator stories.

Nvidia remains the gravity center of the market. The gap with AMD is still too large to frame the market as a simple catch-up story, especially when Nvidia’s data-center revenue is roughly thirteen times larger in the latest comparable results used in the analysis.

The hyperscaler signal is still extremely strong. Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, and Alphabet are not behaving like buyers waiting for a slowdown; their capex and cloud data suggest AI infrastructure demand is still expanding from an already huge base.

The market’s center of excitement is shifting toward inference. Training remains expensive, but inference turns compute into a recurring cost every time users query models, run agents, generate images, or call AI APIs.

Custom AI chips are now a real market, not just internal hyperscaler experiments. Broadcom, Marvell, Google’s TPUs, and hyperscaler-specific silicon all show that workload-specific chips are becoming a serious revenue pool.

The supply shortage has changed shape. The market is no longer only about GPU availability; the tighter constraints now sit in HBM, advanced packaging, power, networking, and full-system deployment.

Memory is one of the clearest hidden winners. HBM and high-capacity server memory are becoming gatekeepers for AI system scale, which makes memory suppliers more strategically important than a normal cyclical recovery story would suggest.

The Nvidia alternative story is working only in narrow forms. AMD clouds, TPUs, custom ASICs, and inference chips matter when they solve a specific buyer pain, but broad “Nvidia killer” narratives still look weak.

China is no longer a clean growth engine for Western AI chip companies. Export controls, Chinese policy signals, and possible tighter enforcement through Taiwan make that demand pool much harder to model.

The final read is that the operating market is stronger than the stock-market setup. AI chip demand is still hot, but investor expectations have become so high that even strong results can disappoint if they do not beat an already aggressive story.

These two Instinct families are really important for AMD's AI strategy moving forward, and the company has reaffirmed its yearly launch cadence to strengthen its AI family against NVIDIA, [which is dominating the segment right now](https://wccftech.com/nvidia-has-already-geared-up-to-challenge-big-tech-custom-ai-chip-ambitions/).

Next year, AMD will launch its [Instinct MI400 series AI accelerators](https://wccftech.com/amd-instinct-mi400-accelerator-doubles-compute-40-pflops-432-gb-hbm4-memory-2026-launch/). The new lineup will be based on the CDNA 5 architecture and offers:

The official metrics list the MI400 as a 40 PFLOP (FP4) & 20 PFLOP (FP8) product, which doubles the compute capability of the MI350 series, which is a hot product for AI data centers.

In addition to the compute capability, AMD is also going to leverage HBM4 memory for its Instinct MI400 series. The new chip will offer a 50% memory capacity uplift from 288GB HBM3e to 432GB HBM4. The HBM4 standard will offer a massive 19.6 TB/s bandwidth, more than double that of the 8 TB/s for the MI350 series. The GPU will also feature a 300 GB/s scale-out bandwidth/per GPU, so some big things are coming in the next generation of Instinct.

# 7 Takeaways from AMD Advancing AI 2026 to Guide Your 2027 Infrastructure Plan

Aug 04, 2026

![Large event banner reads ](/content/dam/amd/en/images/blogs/designs/5210600-aai-data-center-insights.jpg)

Enterprise AI infrastructure planning is changing shape as organizations start shifting more from chatbot-style AI to agentic AI. An AI agent requires a new conversation because it doesn’t just generate a response — it plans, calls tools, queries databases, checks permissions, retrieves memory, and loops, often triggering other agents along the way. Each of those steps still runs on general-purpose compute, which shifts demand across CPU, GPU, networking, and orchestration software at the same time. This forces IT leaders to plan against a new set of criteria. Advancing AI 2026 was where AMD laid out its answer to this shift in detail.

Below are the 7 key takeaways from the event that enterprises should keep in mind when having 2027 infrastructure planning discussions.

### Start With Your Usage Model, Not a Spec Sheet

The first question to answer is not which GPU has the best peak performance, it’s “how does my organization actually use AI?” How many users, how many agents, which models, and how much data needs to stay on-premises for latency or sovereignty reasons? That usage model determines which compute tier you need, in what ratio, and where it should sit.

### Consider the CPU-GPU Ratio Before You Plan the GPU Count

The CPU isn't a supporting actor to the GPU story anymore. In an agentic workload, it's doing real work of its own, and that changes the order in which you should plan. For years, GPU capacity dominated AI infrastructure planning, with the CPU cast as a supporting host node. An agent's workflow breaks that assumption: every plan-call-query-check-retrieve-loop cycle still runs on general-purpose compute, and that workflow splits across distinct profiles that each lean on the CPU differently.

Agent orchestration and sandboxing benefit from CPUs built for that pattern. Host nodes that keep GPU clusters fed during reasoning and inference need a different profile. However, general-purpose enterprise applications (ERP, CRM, the databases agents query to get work done) still need to run somewhere. Planning around a single CPU standard risks under-provisioning at least one of those needs.

At Advancing AI 2026, AMD announced the latest 6th Generation [AMD EPYC™ 9006 Series Server CPUs](/en/products/processors/server/epyc/9006-series.html), the broadest server CPU portfolio built for agentic AI1, spanning cloud, enterprise, general-purpose and HPC workloads. As agent sandboxes, the generation runs the agents, coordinating concurrent agents and executing tasks; as AI host nodes, it keeps accelerators fed with speed and memory bandwidth; as general-purpose servers, it runs business-critical applications and AI support tasks enterprises depend on every day, with enhanced energy efficiency.

The practical implication: size your CPU layer to the workflow first, then size the GPU layer to the model. Getting that order backward is how enterprises end up with GPU clusters that are starved by their own host nodes.

### Match the GPU to Your Buying Scenario

Once you know your usage model and CPU ratio, the GPU decision narrows to the question of which buying scenario you're actually in — not which spec sheet looks best.

Aug 04, 2026

![Large event banner reads ](/content/dam/amd/en/images/blogs/designs/5210600-aai-data-center-insights.jpg)

Enterprise AI infrastructure planning is changing shape as organizations start shifting more from chatbot-style AI to agentic AI. An AI agent requires a new conversation because it doesn’t just generate a response — it plans, calls tools, queries databases, checks permissions, retrieves memory, and loops, often triggering other agents along the way. Each of those steps still runs on general-purpose compute, which shifts demand across CPU, GPU, networking, and orchestration software at the same time. This forces IT leaders to plan against a new set of criteria. Advancing AI 2026 was where AMD laid out its answer to this shift in detail.

Below are the 7 key takeaways from the event that enterprises should keep in mind when having 2027 infrastructure planning discussions.

### Start With Your Usage Model, Not a Spec Sheet

The first question to answer is not which GPU has the best peak performance, it’s “how does my organization actually use AI?” How many users, how many agents, which models, and how much data needs to stay on-premises for latency or sovereignty reasons? That usage model determines which compute tier you need, in what ratio, and where it should sit.

### Consider the CPU-GPU Ratio Before You Plan the GPU Count

The CPU isn't a supporting actor to the GPU story anymore. In an agentic workload, it's doing real work of its own, and that changes the order in which you should plan. For years, GPU capacity dominated AI infrastructure planning, with the CPU cast as a supporting host node. An agent's workflow breaks that assumption: every plan-call-query-check-retrieve-loop cycle still runs on general-purpose compute, and that workflow splits across distinct profiles that each lean on the CPU differently.

Agent orchestration and sandboxing benefit from CPUs built for that pattern. Host nodes that keep GPU clusters fed during reasoning and inference need a different profile. However, general-purpose enterprise applications (ERP, CRM, the databases agents query to get work done) still need to run somewhere. Planning around a single CPU standard risks under-provisioning at least one of those needs.

At Advancing AI 2026, AMD announced the latest 6th Generation [AMD EPYC™ 9006 Series Server CPUs](/en/products/processors/server/epyc/9006-series.html), the broadest server CPU portfolio built for agentic AI1, spanning cloud, enterprise, general-purpose and HPC workloads. As agent sandboxes, the generation runs the agents, coordinating concurrent agents and executing tasks; as AI host nodes, it keeps accelerators fed with speed and memory bandwidth; as general-purpose servers, it runs business-critical applications and AI support tasks enterprises depend on every day, with enhanced energy efficiency.

The practical implication: size your CPU layer to the workflow first, then size the GPU layer to the model. Getting that order backward is how enterprises end up with GPU clusters that are starved by their own host nodes.

Once you know your usage model and CPU ratio, the GPU decision narrows to the question of which buying scenario you're actually in — not which spec sheet looks best.

AMD.overview: AMD offers a full-stack AI compute portfolio that spans data‑center accelerators, server CPUs, edge processors and system‑level solutions. The Instinct line includes the MI400 series GPUs (MI455X and MI430X) with up to 40 PFLOP FP4 performance, the earlier MI300 series and PCIe accelerator cards such as the MI350P. Sixth‑generation EPYC™ server CPUs and the Helios AI rack‑scale platform combine CPUs, GPUs and networking for large‑scale workloads, while Ryzen™ AI Embedded X100 and Kria™ AI SoM address edge and robotics use cases. AMD’s hardware is available through major cloud providers in the United States and Europe and the company has announced a roadmap that extends to the MI500 series and next‑generation EPYC processors.

requirements.requirement: What AI‑focused hardware products (e.g., Radeon Instinct GPUs, EPYC CPUs with AI extensions, accelerators) does AMD currently market for cloud and data‑center AI workloads?

findings.finding: AMD’s AI‑focused hardware portfolio for cloud and data‑center workloads includes the Instinct MI455X and MI430X GPUs (part of the MI400 series), the Instinct MI350P PCIe accelerator cards, 6th‑generation EPYC™ server CPUs, the Helios AI rack‑scale solution, Ryzen™ AI Embedded X100 processors for edge/embedded AI, and the Kria™ AI System‑on‑Module and robotics developer platform.

The Instinct MI400 series, launched in 2026, includes the MI455X GPU for training and inference and the MI430X GPU for HPC. Both deliver up to 40 PFLOP (FP4) and 20 PFLOP (FP8) compute, feature HBM4 memory, and use the CDNA 5 architecture, representing a roughly two‑fold performance increase over the prior MI350 series.
AMD’s MI300 series GPUs, purpose‑built for AI training and inference, have attracted adoption by major cloud providers seeking alternatives to NVIDIA’s offerings.

requirements.summary: AMD’s current AI‑focused hardware for cloud and data‑center workloads includes the Instinct MI455X and MI430X GPUs of the MI400 series, the MI350P PCIe accelerator cards, sixth‑generation EPYC server CPUs, the Helios AI rack‑scale solution, Ryzen AI Embedded X100 processors for edge AI, and Kria AI System‑on‑Module platforms. The MI400 GPUs deliver up to 40 PFLOP (FP4) and 20 PFLOP (FP8) using HBM4 and CDNA 5, roughly doubling performance over the prior MI350 series, while the MI300 series continues to see adoption by cloud providers. These products are marketed as part of AMD’s full‑stack AI compute offering.

findings.finding: AMD announced the Instinct MI500 series of AI accelerators, slated for launch in 2027. Intel Corp.overview: Intel provides a broad AI computing portfolio targeting cloud service providers and AI developers. The lineup includes 4th‑generation Xeon Scalable CPUs, Habana Gaudi AI accelerators (Gaudi 2 and the announced Gaudi 3), and Data Center GPU Flex series GPUs, all supported by the oneAPI and OpenVINO software ecosystems. Intel’s hardware is available through major public clouds such as AWS, Azure, GCP, and IBM Cloud, as well as via private‑network partnerships in the United States and Europe. Pricing is offered through cloud consumption models (on‑demand, reserved, spot, savings plans) and direct hardware pricing, with software toolkits provided under royalty‑free, usage‑based licenses. Intel held an estimated 32 % share of the North American AI compute market in 2025, though European share data are not disclosed.

requirements.requirement: What AI computing products (e.g., Habana Gaudi accelerators, Intel Xe GPUs, Xeon processors with AI extensions) does Intel Corp currently provide for cloud and data‑center AI workloads?

findings.finding: Intel’s AI compute portfolio for data‑center and cloud AI workloads includes its Xeon Scalable processors (including Xeon CPU Max), the Gaudi family of AI accelerators (Gaudi 2 and the newly announced Gaudi 3 PCIe card and 32‑node cluster), Intel Arc Pro GPUs and Data Center GPU Flex series. These products are positioned for both training and inference workloads and are integrated with Intel’s oneAPI and OpenVINO software stack to enable optimized performance. The Gaudi accelerators are offered in a standard PCIe Gen5 form factor and support Ethernet‑based scaling.

Intel currently offers a portfolio of AI compute products for cloud and data‑center workloads, including the 4th Gen Intel Xeon Scalable processors (available on AWS, GCP, Azure), the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series (up to 128 Xe cores, >500 TOPS), the Intel Data Center GPU Flex Series (Flex 140, Flex 170, Flex 170V with 16‑32 Xe cores and an industry‑first AV1 encoder), and a unified software stack via oneAPI toolkits (AI Analytics Toolkit, oneDNN, oneMKL, etc.) that enable optimized AI inference and training across CPUs and GPUs.

requirements.summary: Intel’s AI compute portfolio for cloud and data‑center workloads comprises 4th‑generation Xeon Scalable processors (including Xeon CPU Max), the Habana Gaudi accelerator family (Gaudi 2 and the announced Gaudi 3 PCIe card and 32‑node cluster), Intel Arc Pro GPUs and the Data Center GPU Flex series (Flex 140, Flex 170, Flex 170V). These products support both training and inference and are integrated with Intel’s oneAPI and OpenVINO software stack. The Gaudi accelerators use a PCIe Gen5 form factor with Ethernet‑based scaling, while the GPU Flex line offers up to 128 Xe cores and industry‑first AV1 encoding.

findings.finding: Amazon Web Services (AWS) offers Intel‑based Habana Gaudi AI accelerators through its EC2 DL1 instance type, which is currently available in the United States East (Northern Virginia) and West (Oregon) regions and supports on‑demand, reserved, spot and savings‑plan pricing. IBM Cloud also provides access to Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerators, extending Intel’s AI hardware presence in the cloud (regional coverage not specified). Intel’s partner listings confirm the AWS‑Gaudi integration for the Americas region.

Intel’s 4th Gen Xeon Scalable processors are offered as preview instances on Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud Platform and Microsoft Azure, and are generally available on Alibaba Cloud; benchmark data show deployments on Azure US‑West and US‑East regions, confirming active use in United States data centers. Intel also partners with AWS, Cisco, Ericsson and Nokia to deliver private 5G solutions that incorporate Intel AI hardware, extending availability to Europe and the United States.

Intel also partners with AWS, Cisco, Ericsson and Nokia to deliver private‑network solutions that incorporate its AI chips in both the United States and Europe.

findings.finding: Intel’s AI hardware is monetized through cloud‑based usage models: AWS EC2 DL1 instances powered by Gaudi accelerators are sold on an on‑demand, reserved, spot or savings‑plan basis, providing flexible consumption pricing. Additionally, Intel’s AI software tools are offered under free‑license terms for a limited period, as described in its licensing FAQ.

Intel’s Data Center GPU Flex Series is sold under a recommended‑customer pricing model; Intel cites “up to 50 % lower total‑cost‑of‑ownership for VDI” as of 11 Oct 2023 compared with competing solutions. The oneAPI software toolkits are distributed under the Intel End User License Agreement (EULA) with component‑specific third‑party licenses, providing a royalty‑free, usage‑based licensing model for developers.

requirements.summary: Intel monetizes its AI hardware through cloud‑based consumption models: AWS EC2 DL1 instances with Gaudi accelerators are sold on on‑demand, reserved, spot and savings‑plan pricing, while the Data Center GPU Flex series is sold under a recommended‑customer pricing model that Intel claims can reduce total‑cost‑of‑ownership by up to 50 % for VDI workloads. Its AI software toolkits (oneAPI, AI Analytics Toolkit, etc.) are distributed under the Intel End‑User License Agreement with royalty‑free, usage‑based terms, and some tools are offered free for a limited period.
